content: Dimenhydrinate and ziprasidone both have sedative effects, and their concurrent use may increase sedation. It is essential to exercise caution and closely monitor the patient when these medications are used together. Similarly, dimenhydrinate and zotepine also increase sedation, necessitating careful monitoring and caution during co-administration. The combination of dimenhydrinate and zuranolone is considered serious due to pharmacodynamic synergism, which can amplify the effects of central nervous system (CNS) depression. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use alternative medications. If co-administration is unavoidable, dose reduction should be considered to mitigate risks. The severity and incidence of these effects can vary depending on the specific drug and individual patient susceptibility. CNS-related side effects of dimenhydrinate include drowsiness, sedation (ranging from mild to deep sleep), dizziness, lassitude, disturbed coordination, and muscular weakness. Paradoxical CNS stimulation, such as restlessness, insomnia, tremors, euphoria, nervousness, delirium, palpitations, and seizures, may occur, particularly in children and occasionally in adults. Gastrointestinal side effects include epigastric distress, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Rarely, cholestasis, hepatitis, hepatic failure, abnormal liver function, and jaundice may occur. Dermatological reactions, such as eczema, pruritus, inflammation, papular rash, and erythema, may occur with topical formulations. Cardiovascular effects include tachycardia, palpitations, ECG changes (e.g., widened QRS), arrhythmias (e.g., extrasystole, heart block), hypotension, and hypertension. Geriatric patients may experience dizziness, sedation, and hypotension more frequently. Other side effects include dryness of the mouth, nose, and throat; dysuria; urinary retention; impotence; vertigo; visual disturbances (e.g., blurred vision, diplopia); tinnitus; acute labyrinthitis; insomnia; tremors; nervousness; irritability; facial dyskinesia; chest tightness; thickened bronchial secretions; wheezing; nasal stuffiness; sweating; chills; early menses; toxic psychosis; headache; faintness; and paresthesia. Hematological effects, such as agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia, are rare but documented. Patients with hypersensitivity to dimenhydrinate or diphenhydramine, lower respiratory diseases (e.g., asthma), seizure disorders, angle-closure glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, emphysema, or acute hepatic insufficiency should use this medication with caution. It may impair the ability to drive or operate heavy machinery and can mask early signs of ototoxicity when used with ototoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides). During pregnancy, dimenhydrinate is classified as Category B, indicating no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies. However, it crosses into breast milk and may have undesirable effects on nursing infants. Nursing mothers should either discontinue the drug or avoid breastfeeding. Dimenhydrinate is well absorbed, extensively metabolized in the liver (based on diphenhydramine data), and primarily excreted in the urine as metabolites. Its onset of action is 15–30 minutes orally, 20–30 minutes intramuscularly, and almost immediate intravenously. The duration of action is 3–6 hours. When using liquid forms of dimenhydrinate, measure doses with a proper measuring device or spoon, not a household spoon, to ensure accuracy. The dosage depends on the patient’s age, medical condition, and response to treatment. Common side effects include drowsiness, constipation, blurred vision, and dryness of the mouth, nose, or throat. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, including to dimenhydrinate or diphenhydramine, and disclose all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. Alcohol and marijuana can exacerbate drowsiness caused by this medication, so patients should avoid these substances and refrain from activities requiring alertness, such as driving, until they know how the medication affects them. Dimenhydrinate may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as allergy skin tests, potentially causing false results. In case of overdose, symptoms may include severe drowsiness, seizures, and widened pupils. Emergency medical attention should be sought immediately. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. The medication should be stored at room temperature, away from moisture and light, and not in the bathroom. Liquid forms should not be frozen. Expired or unused medication should be properly discarded, and patients should consult their pharmacist or local waste disposal company for guidance.
